warmup.q: A request thread calls future.get(200, MILLISECONDS) on a task that asks the bank to charge a card. The bank takes 600 ms to answer, so get throws TimeoutException. What happens to the charge?
options: It is cancelled, because the time limit cancels the task
It goes ahead, and the card is charged about 400 ms later
It is undone when TimeoutException is thrown
The task gets a TimeoutException too, and stops
warmup.why: The time limit ends your wait, not the task. Nothing tells the task that you gave up, so it keeps going, and the bank charges the card. To stop it, you must call cancel(true), and even that only sends a request, which the task may or may not notice in time. The first section shows it happening.

opening:
Picture a takeaway counter. You order a burger, pay, and the cashier hands you a ticket with the number 42 on it. The burger doesn't exist yet. The ticket promises that it will, and lets you collect it.

With the ticket, you can do three things. You can wait at the counter until 42 is called. You can wait only five minutes, because your bus is coming. Or you can glance at the screen to see whether it's ready.

Say you give up after five minutes and catch your bus. Nobody tells the kitchen. At minute seven your burger is ready, hot and paid for, with nobody to eat it.

Java's thread pools hand out the same kind of ticket, with the same gap. (A thread pool is a small team of threads, paths of work that run side by side, taking tasks from a queue.) Sizing a pool ended on a question: how do we stop a thread that waits too long? In this lesson, we'll wait for a result with a time limit, ask a task to stop, and keep that request from getting lost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a takeaway counter, with a ticket for a burger nobody came back for. A thread pool hands out the same ticket, a Future. We waited with a time limit and watched the bank charge the card anyway. Three tasks were asked to stop, and only the two that listened did. Then we kept the request alive in a catch block.

Now search your own code for .get( on a Future. Each call should have a time limit, and each TimeoutException should lead to a cancel or a record of the unfinished work.

Next, we'll give a pool a task that comes back on its own, again and again. What happens to it when one run throws?

sections.h: A claim ticket for a result: Callable, Future and a wait with a time limit
sections.html:
Start with a shop's website. When a customer pays, the program asks the bank to charge their card. The bank is another computer, so the program sends a request over the network and waits for the answer. On a normal day, that's about 200 ms. (It's the bank from Sizing a pool.)

We'd like to hand that call to a thread pool and get the answer back. In Why pools, every task was a Runnable, whose run() method returns nothing. A task that should hand back an answer is a Callable<V> instead. Its call() method returns a value of type V, and it may throw any exception, even a checked one.

You give a Callable to the pool with submit, and the pool gives you a Future<V> back at once. A Future is the ticket from the counter: a promise of a result that doesn't exist yet. Here's the smallest one, with a task that just multiplies:

Java
Future<Integer> answer = pool.submit(() -> 6 * 7);   // returns at once, with a ticket
int n = answer.get();                                // waits for the task: 42
Kotlin
val answer: Future<Int> = pool.submit<Int> { 6 * 7 }  // returns at once, with a ticket
val n = answer.get()                                  // waits for the task: 42

get() is the wait at the counter. It blocks: the calling thread stops and does nothing else until the task has finished. Then get() hands over the value.

If the task threw an exception, get() throws an ExecutionException with the task's own exception inside it, as its cause. If someone cancelled the task, it throws CancellationException. And if your own thread is asked to stop while it waits, it throws InterruptedException, which the next two sections are about. (A successful get() also makes everything the task wrote visible to the thread that got the result. The memory model track explains why that matters.)

Plain get() waits as long as the task takes. If the bank takes 30 seconds, your customer waits 30 seconds. So real code waits with a time limit, get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS), which throws TimeoutException if the answer isn't there in time. That's the five minutes before the bus.

Now the trap from the counter. TimeoutDemo, in the Try it below, asks a bank that's having a slow day and takes 600 ms, and it waits only 200 ms. Each line shows the time, the thread and what happened. On a busy machine, it printed:

  86 ms  pool-1-thread-1 asking the bank to charge the card
 285 ms  main         get timed out after 200 ms
 771 ms  pool-1-thread-1 bank answered: APPROVED (the card was charged)
 773 ms  main         pool closed

The main thread gave up at 285 ms. In a real shop, that's the moment the program tells the customer the payment failed. The task didn't know. It kept waiting for the bank, and at 771 ms the bank charged the card. The customer heard "failed" and paid anyway, which is the one combination nobody wants.

So the bank call is the burger at minute seven. A time limit on get ends your wait. It says nothing to the task, which keeps going until it's done.

A time limit ends your wait, not the work. Decide what happens to the work.

You have two choices. Stop the work, or make sure its result is written down somewhere you can find it later. Stopping it means asking the task, and Java's way of asking does less than its name suggests.

try.title: Give up on a slow bank
steps: Run TimeoutDemo in either language. Compare the time on the bank answered line with the time on the get timed out line.
Run it again with -Pargs=cancel. That version calls cancel(true) right after the time limit. Before you run it, predict: does the bank still answer?

code.title: TimeoutDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** get(200 ms) on a call that takes 600 ms. Pass "cancel" to cancel(true) after the timeout. */ public class TimeoutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-12s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> { log("asking the bank to charge the card"); try { Thread.sleep(600); // the bank is slow today } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: giving up on the bank"); throw e; } log("bank answered: APPROVED (the card was charged)"); return "APPROVED"; }); try { log("result: " + auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { log("get timed out after 200 ms"); if (cancel) log("cancel(true) returned " + auth.cancel(true)); } } // close() waits for the task, which is still running unless we cancelled it log("pool closed"); } }

alt.html: package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %-12s %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().name, msg)) /** get(200 ms) on a call that takes 600 ms. Pass "cancel" to cancel(true) after the timeout. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val cancel = args.firstOrNull() == "cancel" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> val auth = pool.submit<String> { log("asking the bank to charge the card") try { Thread.sleep(600) // the bank is slow today } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("interrupted: giving up on the bank") throw e } log("bank answered: APPROVED (the card was charged)") "APPROVED" } try { log("result: " + auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { log("get timed out after 200 ms") if (cancel) log("cancel(true) returned " + auth.cancel(true)) } } // close() waits for the task, which is still running unless we cancelled it log("pool closed") }

try.expect: Without cancel, the bank answers at about 600 to 800 ms, long after get gave up, and the pool closes only then, because close() waits for the task. With cancel, the task prints interrupted: giving up on the bank a few milliseconds after the time limit, cancel(true) returns true, and the pool closes at once. The next section explains why it worked here.

aside.title: Why doesn't a time limit cancel the task for me?
aside.html: One good reason: a ticket can have many people waiting on it. Several threads may call get on the same Future, each with its own time limit. If the first impatient one cancelled the task, the others would lose their result too. And sometimes you still want the result after you stop waiting, for example to record what the bank said. So Future leaves that choice to you: call cancel yourself, when you mean it.

sections.h: Asking the kitchen to stop: cancel(true) sends an interrupt, nothing more
sections.html:
The cancel run of TimeoutDemo looked easy. We cancelled, and the task stopped within a few milliseconds. Here it is, from the same busy machine:

  60 ms  pool-1-thread-1 asking the bank to charge the card
 257 ms  main         get timed out after 200 ms
 260 ms  pool-1-thread-1 interrupted: giving up on the bank
 275 ms  main         cancel(true) returned true
 280 ms  main         pool closed

To see why it worked, and when it won't, we need to know what cancel actually does.

Future.cancel(boolean mayInterruptIfRunning) has two modes. cancel(false) stops a task that hasn't started yet, so it never runs, and leaves a running task alone. cancel(true) does the same, and if the task is running, it also interrupts the thread that runs it.

An interrupt is a request to a thread to stop what it's doing. It sets a true-or-false value inside the thread, called the interrupt flag. If the thread is blocked at that moment, waiting in a method such as Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue.take or Future.get, that method wakes up and throws InterruptedException. If the thread is busy computing, nothing happens to it. The flag stays set until the thread looks at it.

Setting the flag is all cancel(true) does. Java has no safe way to kill a thread from outside. Thread.stop() was deprecated, marked as "don't use", for decades, has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since JDK 20, and was removed in JDK 26. So cancelling is cooperative: it works only if the task helps.

Picture the interrupt as a note that the manager puts on a cook's station: "please stop order 42". Our kitchen has three cooks. The first is waiting for the oven. The second is chopping onions, and looks up after each one. The third is chopping too, and never looks up.

The task in TimeoutDemo was the first cook. It was waiting in Thread.sleep, which stands in for the wait for the bank's answer, so the note woke it at once.

CancelDemo builds all three cooks in code. The sleeper sleeps. The checker does 400 slices of arithmetic, a few milliseconds each, and checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() before each slice. The ignorer does the same work and never checks. After 100 ms, main calls cancel(true) on all three:

after cancel: isCancelled=true/true/true isDone=true/true/true
sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping
checker: saw the flag after 51 slices, stopping
ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway, 769 ms after the cancel
pool closed

Read the first line again. All three futures said cancelled and done straight away, before any task had reacted. A Future changes its state the moment you call cancel. It doesn't wait for the task to stop.

Then each cook did what that cook does. The sleeper, waiting for the oven, was woken by the note. The checker saw it the next time it looked up. The ignorer chopped on for another 769 ms, as if nobody had said a word. If its work had been charging a card, the card would be charged, under a ticket that says cancelled.

Here the kitchen picture breaks in two places. A real cook hears you shout across the room, but a thread hears nothing unless it's waiting or it looks. And a real kitchen can tell you whether the dish was made. A cancelled Future can't. It only knows that nobody will collect a result.

Cancelling only asks. The task must listen, and the ticket can't tell you whether it did.

So a long computing loop should look up now and then, as the checker does. In the Try it, you'll teach the ignorer that habit.

cancel(false) has its own use. When a program shuts down, you may want running tasks to finish but queued ones never to start. Cancel the queued ones with false. And cancel returns false if the task had already finished or was already cancelled, which tells you the request came too late.

The sleeper stopped because sleep threw InterruptedException. What a task does with that exception decides whether the stop request survives.

try.title: Cancel three kinds of task
steps: Run CancelDemo and match each line of the output to one of the three cooks.
Teach the ignorer to look up: copy the checker's isInterrupted() check, with its return, into the ignorer's loop. Predict how long after the cancel it stops now, then run it.

code.title: CancelDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ public class CancelDemo { static volatile long sink; // keeps each result, so the JIT can't skip the work static volatile long cancelledAt; // when main called cancel, for the ignorer's report // a few milliseconds of CPU work: 400 of them take a second or more static long slice(long x) { for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) x = x * 31 + i; return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { Future<?> sleeper = pool.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(5_000); System.out.println("sleeper: woke up normally"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping"); } }); Future<?> checker = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { System.out.println("checker: saw the flag after " + s + " slices, stopping"); return; } x = slice(x); } sink = x; System.out.println("checker: finished all 400 slices"); }); Future<?> ignorer = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) x = slice(x); // never looks at the flag sink = x; long late = (System.nanoTime() - cancelledAt) / 1_000_000; System.out.println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway, " + late + " ms after the cancel"); }); Thread.sleep(100); cancelledAt = System.nanoTime(); for (Future<?> f : new Future<?>[] {sleeper, checker, ignorer}) f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b%n", sleeper.isCancelled(), checker.isCancelled(), ignorer.isCancelled(), sleeper.isDone(), checker.isDone(), ignorer.isDone()); } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU System.out.println("pool closed"); } }

alt.title: CancelDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors @Volatile private var sink = 0L // keeps each result, so the JIT can't skip the work @Volatile private var cancelledAt = 0L // when main called cancel, for the ignorer's report // a few milliseconds of CPU work: 400 of them take a second or more private fun slice(start: Long): Long { var x = start for (i in 0 until 2_000_000) x = x * 31 + i return x } /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> val sleeper = pool.submit { try { Thread.sleep(5_000) println("sleeper: woke up normally") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping") } } val checker = pool.submit { var x = 0L for (s in 0 until 400) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { println("checker: saw the flag after $s slices, stopping") return@submit } x = slice(x) } sink = x println("checker: finished all 400 slices") } val ignorer = pool.submit { var x = 0L repeat(400) { x = slice(x) } // never looks at the flag sink = x val late = (System.nanoTime() - cancelledAt) / 1_000_000 println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway, $late ms after the cancel") } Thread.sleep(100) cancelledAt = System.nanoTime() listOf(sleeper, checker, ignorer).forEach { it.cancel(true) } println("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b".format( sleeper.isCancelled, checker.isCancelled, ignorer.isCancelled, sleeper.isDone, checker.isDone, ignorer.isDone)) } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU println("pool closed") }

try.expect: First run: the sleeper and the checker stop within a few milliseconds of the cancel. The ignorer runs on for hundreds of milliseconds (769 ms in the run above, on a busy machine), and close() waits for it, so pool closed comes last. After your change, the ignorer stops after a few dozen slices too, and pool closed follows the cancel almost at once.

sections.h: Keeping the stop request alive: rethrow InterruptedException or restore the flag
sections.html:
Here's a task that does almost everything right. StatementPoller, from this lesson's lab, asks the bank every so often for new lines on an account statement, the list of money in and out of an account. It runs as a task on a pool. It should stop when someone shuts the pool down with shutdownNow(), or cancels the task with cancel(true). Both of those interrupt its thread. Here's its starting code:

Java
// Naive: the stop request is lost in pause()
public void run() {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        pollOnce.run();
        polls.incrementAndGet();
        pause();
    }
}

private void pause() {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(interval.toMillis());
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        // nothing useful to do here; the loop will carry on
    }
}
Kotlin
// Naive: the stop request is lost in pause()
override fun run() {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) {
        pollOnce.run()
        polls.incrementAndGet()
        pause()
    }
}

private fun pause() {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(interval.toMillis())
    } catch (e: InterruptedException) {
        // nothing useful to do here; the loop will carry on
    }
}

(The lab is in Java. The Kotlin version is a translation, so you can read it in either language.)

The loop checks the flag on every pass, so it looks right. Yet in the lab's tests, shutdownNow() returns, awaitTermination (which waits for the pool to finish) runs out its full five seconds, and the poller keeps polling. Let's follow one stop request through it, step by step:

  1. The poller is asleep in Thread.sleep, where it spends nearly all its time.
  2. The test calls shutdownNow() on the pool, which interrupts the poller's thread.
  3. sleep wakes up. Before it throws InterruptedException, it clears the interrupt flag.
  4. pause() catches the exception, does nothing, and returns.
  5. The loop checks isInterrupted(). The flag is clear, so the check reads false, and the poller polls again.

Nobody interrupts it a second time, so it never stops.

Step 3 is the one people miss. In A thread's life, the interrupt was a note on a clerk's desk, and waking up tore the note off. Inside the catch block, you hold the only copy of the request. If you drop it, no code further up can ever see it.

So there are two correct moves. Let the exception travel up to your caller, or put the note back with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before you go on. Here they are on a task that clips a ticket onto the kitchen's rail, a BlockingQueue whose put waits while the rail is full:

Java
// 1. propagate: declare it and let it go up
void clip(Ticket t) throws InterruptedException {
    rail.put(t);
}

// 2. you can't propagate (Runnable.run can't throw it): restore the flag
public void run() {
    try {
        rail.put(ticket);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // put the request back
        return;                               // and stop
    }
}
Kotlin
// 1. propagate: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so simply don't catch it
fun clip(t: Ticket) {
    rail.put(t)
}

// 2. if you do catch it: restore the flag
override fun run() {
    try {
        rail.put(ticket)
    } catch (e: InterruptedException) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt()    // put the request back
        return                                // and stop
    }
}

Wrapping it in an exception of your own is fine, as long as you restore the flag first. Logging it and moving on is not. From JDK 26, the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that states this same rule.

A swallowed interrupt makes shutdownNow() and cancel(true) do nothing. Rethrow it, or restore it.

A request can get lost in one more place: a thread waiting for another computer's answer. Whether that thread notices an interrupt depends on how it reads from the network. A read through a channel from java.nio.channels, Java's newer networking classes, does notice: the JDK closes the channel and the read fails. A read from a classic java.net.Socket on a platform thread, an ordinary operating-system thread, doesn't notice and waits on. So give every call to another computer its own time limit, and treat the interrupt as a second line of defense.

Check yourself before you go on. A task catches InterruptedException from sleep, logs it, and goes back to sleep. Does the second sleep throw at once? No. The flag was cleared, so it sleeps its full time. Add Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to the catch, and the second sleep throws straight away, because sleep checks the flag before it starts to wait.

The stop request survives now. One part of the ticket is still clumsy, though: to find out how a task ended, we call get() and catch every exception it can throw.

sections.h: Reading the ticket without waiting: Future.state(), invokeAll and invokeAny
sections.html:
Before JDK 19, the only way to ask a Future how its task ended was to call get() inside a try, with a catch for each outcome. JDK 19 added state(), the glance at the screen. It never blocks, and it returns one of four values: RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED. Two more methods read a finished ticket without any checked exceptions:

Java
switch (f.state()) {
    case RUNNING   -> log.info("still waiting for the bank");
    case SUCCESS   -> record(f.resultNow());                           // the value
    case FAILED    -> log.warn("bank call failed", f.exceptionNow());  // the task's own exception
    case CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled");
}
Kotlin
when (f.state()) {
    Future.State.RUNNING -> log.info("still waiting for the bank")
    Future.State.SUCCESS -> record(f.resultNow())                          // the value
    Future.State.FAILED -> log.warn("bank call failed", f.exceptionNow())  // the task's own exception
    Future.State.CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled")
}

resultNow() gives you the value, and exceptionNow() gives you the task's own exception, without the ExecutionException around it. Both are for tickets you know are finished.

resultNow() throws IllegalStateException if the task isn't done or didn't succeed. exceptionNow() throws it if the task didn't fail, and a cancelled task didn't fail. So check state() first, as the switch does. The lab's Futures.describe is this switch, turned into one line for a log.

A pool can also handle a whole list of tickets for you. Picture phoning three shops to ask whether they have an item in stock, and taking the first "yes". ExecutorService, the interface every pool in this track implements, has two methods for jobs like that:

  • invokeAll(tasks) runs every task and returns all their futures once every one has finished. With a time limit, it cancels whatever isn't done by then, so every future it returns is finished.
  • invokeAny(tasks) returns the result of the first task that succeeds. It cancels the rest, and it throws ExecutionException only if every task fails.

InvokeAnyDemo asks three exchange-rate services for today's rate from euros to US dollars, that is, how many dollars one euro buys. Alpha takes 300 ms. Beta takes 100 ms and then fails. Gamma takes 200 ms. Before reading on, guess what invokeAny returns:

invokeAny -> gamma EUR/USD 1.0842
  alpha: interrupted, cancelled
invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:
  alpha: interrupted, cancelled
  CANCELLED
  FAILED: beta is down
  SUCCESS: gamma EUR/USD 1.0842

Beta answered first, and its answer was that it was down. A failure doesn't count as an answer, so invokeAny waited for gamma, took its rate, and interrupted alpha, which was still on the phone. Then invokeAll, with a 250 ms deadline, returned one ticket of each kind: alpha cancelled at the deadline, beta failed, gamma succeeded.

Both methods block the thread that calls them until they return. So call them from a thread that is allowed to wait, never from a task running on the same small pool.

Here's why. Picture a pool of 3 threads, running 3 tasks that each call invokeAll with 3 subtasks on that same pool. All three threads now wait for subtasks, and no thread is free to run one. Nothing ever moves again. Lesson 9 of this track calls that pool-induced deadlock, and has you fix one.

state() reads a ticket without waiting. Check it before you call resultNow().

We now have the whole ticket: collect it, wait with a limit, cancel it, read it at a glance. What a ticket can't do is come back on its own, every few seconds, all day.

try.title: First good answer wins
steps: Read the three services in InvokeAnyDemo: alpha takes 300 ms, beta fails after 100 ms, gamma takes 200 ms. Predict what invokeAny returns and which service gets interrupted.
Predict the three states that invokeAll reports with its 250 ms deadline. Then run the demo.

code.title: InvokeAnyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ public class InvokeAnyDemo { static Callable<String> provider(String name, long millis, boolean fails) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(millis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": interrupted, cancelled"); throw e; } if (fails) throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is down"); return name + " EUR/USD 1.0842"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<Callable<String>> providers = List.of( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false)); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { System.out.println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:"); List<Future<String>> all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); for (Future<String> f : all) { System.out.println(" " + f.state() + switch (f.state()) { case SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow(); case FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().getMessage(); default -> ""; }); } } } }

alt.title: InvokeAnyDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Future import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private fun provider(name: String, millis: Long, fails: Boolean) = Callable { try { Thread.sleep(millis) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println(" $name: interrupted, cancelled") throw e } if (fails) throw IllegalStateException("$name is down") "$name EUR/USD 1.0842" } /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ fun main() { val providers = listOf( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false), ) Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)) Thread.sleep(50) println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:") val all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) for (f in all) { val detail = when (f.state()) { Future.State.SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow() Future.State.FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().message else -> "" } println(" ${f.state()}$detail") } } }

try.expect: invokeAny returns gamma's rate. Beta finished first, but it failed, and a failure doesn't count. Alpha prints interrupted, cancelled. With the 250 ms deadline, invokeAll reports alpha CANCELLED (interrupted at the deadline), beta FAILED with beta is down, and gamma SUCCESS.

compare.title: Cancelling work: a Future and an interrupt vs a coroutine

java.title: CancelOne.java
java.html: Future<String> f = pool.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(5_000); // wakes with InterruptedException on cancel(true) return "done"; }); Thread.sleep(100); f.cancel(true); // sends an interrupt to the worker thread // f.isCancelled() is true at once, whatever the task does next

kotlin.title: CancelOne.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(5_000) // pauses; resumes with CancellationException on cancel println("done") } delay(100) job.cancel() // no interrupt: delay() notices the cancellation itself // a blocking call ignores job.cancel() unless you wrap it: // runInterruptible { Thread.sleep(5_000) }

compare.note: Both versions ask, and neither can force. Java sends the request as an interrupt, which blocking methods and isInterrupted() checks pick up. Kotlin's coroutines, light tasks that can pause without holding a thread, get it as a CancellationException at the points where they pause, such as delay, await and withContext. No interrupt is involved, so a blocking Java call inside a coroutine doesn't notice the cancel unless you wrap it in runInterruptible. The interrupt rules from this lesson still apply to Kotlin code that runs blocking work on an executor. Watch runCatching there: it catches InterruptedException like any other exception, which makes it an easy way to swallow a stop request. The coroutines track covers cancellation in full.

worked.title: Give up on a slow bank without telling the customer something wrong

steps.say: A payment handler hands the bank call to a pool and waits for the answer. On a normal day, this works. Before reading on, decide what happens when the bank starts taking 30 seconds to answer.
steps.code: Future<String> charge = pool.submit(() -> bank.charge(payment)); return charge.get(); // waits as long as the bank does

alt.html: val charge = pool.submit<String> { bank.charge(payment) } return charge.get() // waits as long as the bank does

steps.say: Every request thread ends up stuck in get(). Little's law, from Sizing a pool, does the rest: at 400 payments a second and 30 seconds each, 12,000 requests are inside at once, each holding a thread. The program stops answering anyone. So wait with a time limit, and cancel the work you stopped waiting for.
steps.code: Future<String> charge = pool.submit(() -> bank.charge(payment)); try { return charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // 1. wait, with a limit } catch (TimeoutException e) { charge.cancel(true); // 2. ask the bank call to stop return "PENDING"; // 3. don't claim it failed }

alt.html: val charge = pool.submit<String> { bank.charge(payment) } return try { charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. wait, with a limit } catch (e: TimeoutException) { charge.cancel(true) // 2. ask the bank call to stop "PENDING" // 3. don't claim it failed }

steps.say: Why PENDING and not DECLINED? The request may have reached the bank before the interrupt arrived, and a classic socket read may not even notice the interrupt. So the card may still be charged. If we said "declined", the customer would pay again, and then they'd have paid twice.

Make the outcome easy to find later. Give every payment a unique ID and send it with the request, so the bank charges each ID at most once, however many times it hears it. On a timeout, add the ID to a list that a small job works through later, asking the bank what happened to each one. (Engineers call an ID like this an idempotency key: sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once.)
steps.code: String paymentId = payment.id(); Future<String> charge = pool.submit(() -> bank.charge(payment, paymentId)); try { return charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { charge.cancel(true); checkLater.add(paymentId); // 4. a later job asks the bank about it return "PENDING"; }

alt.html: val paymentId = payment.id() val charge = pool.submit<String> { bank.charge(payment, paymentId) } return try { charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { charge.cancel(true) checkLater.add(paymentId) // 4. a later job asks the bank about it "PENDING" }

lab.title: Time limits, states and a poller that won't stop
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail.
Write Futures.getOrDefault. Call get with the time limit, and write one catch for each outcome in the Javadoc. On a timeout, and when your own thread is interrupted, call cancel(true) first.
Write Futures.describe as a switch on future.state(), using resultNow() and exceptionNow().
StatementPoller is the starting code from the third section. Run its two tests and read the failure: the pool never finishes. Fix the line that loses the stop request, with one statement.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: get(long, TimeUnit) can end in four ways here besides success: TimeoutException, ExecutionException, CancellationException and InterruptedException. One multi-catch handles the two that get the same answer.
In getOrDefault, after you cancel on InterruptedException, throw the same exception again. Passing it up is one of the two correct moves, so you don't also need to restore the flag.
The poller's while condition is fine. Ask what state the interrupt flag is in when that condition runs, right after pause() caught an InterruptedException.

drill.title: A polling loop that stops when asked
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Runnable that calls poll() once a second until its thread is interrupted, then returns. It must stop whether the interrupt arrives during poll() or during the sleep. Then compare with the answer. Did you restore the flag, or return straight from the catch? Both work.

answer.title: Poller.java
answer.html: Runnable poller = () -> { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { // interrupt during poll(): seen here poll(); try { Thread.sleep(1_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { // interrupt during sleep: flag now cleared Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore it (or simply return) } } };

alt.title: Poller.kt
alt.html: val poller = Runnable { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { // interrupt during poll(): seen here poll() try { Thread.sleep(1_000) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { // interrupt during sleep: flag now cleared Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // restore it (or simply return) } } }

recap: submit(Callable) hands back a Future, a claim ticket, at once. get returns the value, or throws ExecutionException, CancellationException or InterruptedException.
get with a time limit ends your wait, not the task. Cancel the work, or make its outcome findable later, for example with a unique payment ID.
cancel(true) only interrupts. The task stops if it's blocked in a method that listens for interrupts, or if it checks isInterrupted(). The Future says cancelled either way.
Throwing InterruptedException clears the flag. Rethrow it, or restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Never swallow it.
JDK 19 added state(), resultNow() and exceptionNow(). invokeAll waits for every task, and invokeAny returns the first success and cancels the rest.
The limit: a Future can only be waited on, read or cancelled. Nothing here runs a task again later, or on a timetable. That's the next lesson.

explain.prompt: A teammate's code has catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted, retrying"); } inside a retry loop. Explain why this stops the program from shutting down cleanly, and what they should write instead.
explain.answer: When a waiting method like sleep or take throws InterruptedException, it clears the thread's interrupt flag first. So once the catch logs and retries, nothing remembers that someone asked the loop to stop. When the pool calls shutdownNow, or someone calls cancel(true), this task just keeps retrying. awaitTermination runs out of time, and in the end the program gets killed in the middle of its work. They should either let the exception travel up, by declaring throws InterruptedException, or, if the method can't throw it, call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in the catch and then stop the loop or throw a different exception. Then any code above them that checks the flag still sees the request.

deeper.html:
Two methods read the interrupt flag, and they are easy to mix up. Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() reads it and leaves it alone. The static Thread.interrupted() reads it and clears it. Use the second only when you are about to handle the interrupt yourself, for example to throw InterruptedException from a blocking method of your own:

Java
if (Thread.interrupted()) throw new InterruptedException();   // clear, then report by throwing
Kotlin
if (Thread.interrupted()) throw InterruptedException()        // clear, then report by throwing

How does cancel(true) find the thread? submit wraps your task in a FutureTask, and the FutureTask remembers the thread that is running it. cancel(true) moves the task to its cancelled state and then calls interrupt() on that thread.

The flag belongs to the thread, not to the task, so a pool has to make sure an interrupt meant for one task doesn't hit the next task on the same thread. ThreadPoolExecutor does that: before each task, its worker clears any leftover interrupt, unless the pool itself is stopping after shutdownNow().

Virtual threads, in the "Virtual threads" track, use the same interrupt mechanism. A virtual thread waiting in sleep or in a BlockingQueue responds exactly as described here, so everything in this lesson carries over.
